subject: zoology
question_text: Which arthropod is called a 'living fossil'? Name its respiratory organs.

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.53, VSAQ 94). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The living fossil
steps.why: A living fossil is defined by the comparison with its own fossils, so the reason has to be written and not only the name.
common_mistakes: Naming the cockroach. The living fossil arthropod is Limulus.
Writing only the name. One line of reason is expected as well.
steps.memory_tip: Limulus, the king crab: an old design that is still alive.
steps.margin_note: Name the animal, then one line saying why it carries the name.
lines: Limulus, the king crab, is the arthropod
It belongs to the subphylum Chelicerata.
It is called a living fossil because it has
changed very little from its fossil ancestors,
and its close relatives are all extinct.

steps.label: Its respiratory organs
steps.why: The name of the organ describes its shape, so a student who pictures a stack of plates will not confuse book gills with the tracheae of an insect.
common_mistakes: Writing book lungs. Book lungs are aerial and belong to the scorpion; Limulus is aquatic and has book gills.
Writing gills alone. The organ has a name of its own: book gills.
steps.memory_tip: Limulus lives in water, so gills. The scorpion lives on land, so lungs.
steps.margin_note: Name the organ, then one line on where it lies. Two or three lines.
lines: The respiratory organs of Limulus are book
They are flat plates of gill tissue stacked
one over another like the pages of a book,
and they lie on the abdominal appendages.
Limulus is aquatic, so its book gills take up
the oxygen dissolved in the water.

insider_note: Both halves of this question are one word each, so nothing is gained by writing more — but 'gills' without the word 'book' has cost students the second mark.
